meta.title: Who originally recorded "Cry Baby"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Janis Joplin. Garnet Mimms & the Enchanters cut “Cry Baby” first, in 1963 on United Artists — No. 1 R&B, No. 4 pop.
meta.ogDescription: Janis Joplin's 1971 Pearl version is a cover. Garnet Mimms & the Enchanters recorded it first in 1963 and took it to No. 1 R&B.

answer.label: Not a Janis Joplin original — a 1963 Garnet Mimms & the Enchanters single on United Artists
answer.originalArtistDates: Garnet Mimms, b. 16 November 1933, Ashland, West Virginia · American soul and gospel singer · the Enchanters formed 1961 in Philadelphia
answer.sourceLine: Janis Joplin’s reading of “Cry Baby” is so total that most people assume she made the record from nothing. She didn’t. The song was written by Bert Berns and Jerry Ragovoy and first recorded by Garnet Mimms and the Enchanters ↗, issued as a United Artists single on 5 August 1963 with Berns producing. Far from an obscure demo, the Mimms original topped the R&B chart and reached No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100. Joplin’s version was cut in 1970 and released on the posthumous album Pearl, seven years after the record it was covering.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: United Artists
original.released: Issued as a 7-inch single on United Artists on 5 August 1963, credited to Garnet Mimms and the Enchanters, backed with “Don’t Change Your Heart.” Bert Berns produced.
original.charted: A major hit on release: No. 1 on the R&B chart and No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100, with No. 5 placings reported in Canada and New Zealand.
original.cover: Janis Joplin recorded it in 1970 with producer Paul A. Rothchild for Pearl, released by Columbia Records on 11 January 1971 after her death on 4 October 1970. Columbia issued it as a single on 23 April 1971 backed with “Mercedes Benz”; it reached No. 42 on the Billboard Hot 100.

trail: The song’s own reference article is filed under the original artist, not the famous one: Cry Baby (Garnet Mimms song) ↗, which dates the United Artists single to 5 August 1963 and names Berns and Ragovoy as writers.
Both writers hid behind pen names on the label — Berns as “Bert Russell,” Ragovoy as “Norman Meade” — a habit Ragovoy ↗ also used on “Time Is on My Side.”
The Bert Berns estate’s own account ↗ places the record at the front of the soul revolution, calling it a gospelised production that stood apart from everything around it.
MusicBrainz carries the 1963 United States single as a distinct recording entity, credited to Garnet Mimms & the Enchanters ↗.

authors.name: Garnet Mimms and the Enchanters
authors.heading: Who actually cut it first
authors.metaLine: Garnet Mimms, b. 16 November 1933 · American soul singer · group formed 1961
authors.bio: Born Garrett Mimms in Ashland, West Virginia and raised in Philadelphia on church choirs and gospel groups, Mimms formed the Enchanters in 1961 and moved the group to New York in 1963, where they fell in with Bert Berns and Jerry Ragovoy. “Cry Baby” was the result, and it made him one of the first singers to carry an unmistakably gospel intensity onto the pop chart. He kept recording through the 1960s and 1970s, then turned to gospel ministry in the 1980s before returning to music in 2007.

authors.name: Janis Joplin
authors.heading: The version everyone knows
authors.bio: Joplin recorded “Cry Baby” in 1970 with the Full Tilt Boogie Band and producer Paul A. Rothchild during the sessions for Pearl, an album she did not live to finish; she died on 4 October 1970 and Columbia released the record the following January. Her performance is one of the great vocal readings in rock, and the reason the song is still in circulation at all. The only thing wrong with the popular story is the chronology — she was covering a seven-year-old hit, not writing a new one.

authors.name: Bert Berns and Jerry Ragovoy
authors.heading: Who wrote it
authors.metaLine: Bert Berns, 1929–1967 · Jerry Ragovoy, 1930–2011 · American songwriters and producers
authors.bio: Berns and Ragovoy were two of the architects of 1960s soul, and both wrote under aliases — Berns as Bert Russell, Ragovoy as Norman Meade. Between them they are responsible for “Twist and Shout,” “Piece of My Heart,” “Time Is on My Side” and “Stay with Me.” Berns also produced the Mimms session; he died of heart failure in 1967 at 38, and Ragovoy went on to found the Hit Factory in New York before his death in 2011.

misattribution.heading: The record, corrected
misattribution.intro: This is a chronology error, not a credit dispute. Nobody claims Joplin wrote “Cry Baby” — the writers are on every label — but a great many listeners assume the record began with her.

items.why: Her Pearl version is so definitive that the song is filed under her name in most people’s memory.
Recorded and released first, on United Artists, 5 August 1963 — a No. 1 R&B and No. 4 pop hit in its own right.
Credited on both versions, though on the 1963 label as Bert Russell and Norman Meade.

misattribution.truthLine: Right song, right singer, wrong order: Joplin’s 1971 recording is a cover of a 1963 Garnet Mimms and the Enchanters hit.

context.heading: Why the cover swallowed the original
lead: The interesting question is not how Joplin’s version got big — it is how a No. 1 R&B and No. 4 pop record disappeared behind it. Part of the answer is format. The Mimms original was a single, the currency of 1963, and singles are consumed and discarded; Joplin’s was a track on Pearl, an album that went to No. 1 on the Billboard 200 and stayed there for nine weeks and has been in print ever since. An album keeps reintroducing itself. A seven-inch does not.

The rest of the answer is death. Joplin died on 4 October 1970 and Pearl arrived on 11 January 1971 as the last word from an artist who had none left to give, which is a story radio and memory both find irresistible. Mimms, meanwhile, kept working, moved into gospel ministry in the 1980s, and never had a myth attached to him. The record survived; the credit migrated.
detailsBody: 1961 — Garnet Mimms forms the Enchanters in Philadelphia with Sam Bell, Charles Boyer and Zola Pearnell.
1963 — The group relocates to New York and begins working with Bert Berns and Jerry Ragovoy.
5 August 1963 — “Cry Baby” is issued as a United Artists single, produced by Berns, backed with “Don’t Change Your Heart.”
1963 — The single tops the R&B chart and reaches No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100.
1970 — Janis Joplin records the song with producer Paul A. Rothchild during the Pearl sessions at Sunset Sound in Hollywood.
4 October 1970 — Joplin dies, leaving the album unfinished.
11 January 1971 — Columbia releases Pearl; it reaches No. 1 on the Billboard 200.
23 April 1971 — “Cry Baby” is issued as a Columbia single backed with “Mercedes Benz” and reaches No. 42 on the Hot 100.
context.pull: A hit single is a moment. A posthumous album is a monument.
